lessons.t: The autonomy dial: suggest, draft, act with approval, act
lessons.html:
Chapter 6 introduced autonomy levels as the most important line in an agent spec. This lesson is about choosing the level, and designing the experience at each one. The dial has four settings:

LevelWhat the AI doesWhat the user doesCost when the AI is wrongExamples
SuggestOffers an option inlineAccepts, ignores or editsNear zero; the user ignores itCode completion, smart reply, autocomplete for a filter
DraftProduces a complete artefact the user ownsReviews and sends or savesThe user’s review time, plus anything they missEmail draft, PR description, first cut of a report
Act with approvalPrepares an action and waitsApproves, edits or rejects each action or batchApproval fatigue; rubber-stampingAgent proposes a refund, a calendar change, a shell command
ActExecutes and reportsMonitors, interrupts, undoesWhatever the action did before anyone noticedAuto-triage of tickets, background coding agent opening a PR

Choose a level for each action

One feature usually contains actions at several levels. A support agent might act on look-ups, draft replies, and ask approval for refunds. Set the level for each action class from four inputs:

  • Reversibility. Can it be undone fully, cheaply and quickly?
  • Blast radius. Who is affected: one user, a customer, everyone?
  • Verification cost. How long does it take a person to check the output properly?
  • Measured reliability. pass^k on your eval for this action (Chapter 5), never a demo.
Cheap to verifyExpensive to verify
ReversibleAct, with visible undoAct with approval at batch level, or draft
IrreversibleAct with approval per actionDraft or suggest; a human takes the action

Approval is not the same as oversight

Anthropic’s February 2026 study of Claude Code usage found that users with fewer than 50 sessions fully auto-approved about 20% of the time, rising above 40% by 750 sessions. The same experienced users also interrupted more often, in about 9% of turns against about 5% for newer users. Oversight moved from approving every step to watching and stepping in. Anthropic’s conclusion was that products should give trustworthy visibility and easy intervention, and should not force per-action approval that adds friction without clear safety benefit.

The rubber-stamp test

If users approve more than about 95% of prompts at a given step (an illustrative threshold), the approval is no longer a check. Either the step is safe enough to automate with undo, or it is risky enough to need a better review surface. Track approval rate and time-to-approve per step.

Let users move the dial

Start conservative, and let users raise autonomy per action class as they gain confidence: “always allow this command in this project”, “send replies to this customer without asking”. Make the current setting visible and easy to lower. Never raise it silently after a model upgrade.

What changes for you

  • In every AI spec, list each action class with its autonomy level and the reason: reversibility, blast radius, verification cost and measured reliability.
  • Instrument approval rate and time-to-approve per step. Redesign any step that is approved almost every time in a few seconds.
  • Design the intervention controls (pause, stop, redirect, undo) as first-class features, with the same care as the happy path.

lessons.t: Calibrating trust: sources, uncertainty and showing work
lessons.html:
The goal is appropriate reliance: users accept the output when it is right and catch it when it is wrong. Too little trust and nobody uses the feature. Too much, and users accept errors they would have caught on their own. Microsoft Research’s literature review on overreliance defines the failure as users accepting incorrect AI output, and warns that human oversight often makes the user the last line of defence. Later work from the same group found that some mitigations backfire. So judge every trust device by whether it helps users catch errors. Whether users like it is a separate question.

Three levers

LeverHelps whenFails whenDesign note
Sources and citationsAnswers rest on documents the user can openCitations look authoritative but do not support the claimLink to the exact passage; eval citation support separately from answer quality
Uncertainty signalsThe system can detect weak evidence or disagreementA model’s own stated confidence is poorly calibratedPrefer behaviour (abstaining, asking, showing “no source found”) to a percentage
Showing workThe user can check steps faster than redo the taskThe trace is long, technical or decorativeShow the plan, actions taken, what was checked, and a diff of changes

Sources

A citation is a promise that the source says what the answer says. Break that promise once and users stop checking, or stop trusting. Treat citation accuracy as its own eval metric (Chapter 5): for a sample of answers, does each cited passage support the sentence it is attached to? Show sources inline next to the claim, open to the relevant passage, and say clearly when an answer draws on the model’s general knowledge with no source.

Uncertainty

Asking a model “how confident are you?” gives you a fluent number that tracks correctness loosely at best. Better signals come from the system: retrieval found nothing relevant, several samples disagree, a validator rejected the output, the request is outside the documented scope. Turn those signals into behaviour the user can see: ask a clarifying question, return a partial answer with the gap named, or decline that part. Microsoft’s Human-AI Interaction guidelines put it plainly as two early rules: make clear what the system can do, and how well it can do it.

Showing work

For agents, the trace is the trust surface. Show what the agent plans to do, what it did, and what it verified. Summarise first and let users expand. Make verification cheap: a diff for edits, the rows changed in a spreadsheet, the exact message before it sends. An explanation that sounds convincing can raise acceptance of wrong answers as well as right ones, so prefer evidence the user can check over reasons the model gives.

The metric that matters

Split acceptance by correctness. Accept-when-right shows usefulness. Accept-when-wrong shows overreliance. You need labelled samples (from evals or seeded errors in user tests) to compute the second, and it is the number to drive down.

What changes for you

  • Add citation accuracy and accept-when-wrong rate to the feature’s eval and dashboard.
  • Specify behaviours for low-confidence states (ask, abstain, partial answer) in place of a confidence score in the UI.
  • Review every agent surface for one question: can a user verify the result faster than doing the task themselves? If not, redesign the review view.

lessons.t: Failure UX: recovery, undo and graceful refusal
lessons.html:
An AI feature will be wrong in production. The design question is what happens next. Good failure UX makes errors cheap to notice, cheap to fix and safe to retry. Google’s People + AI Guidebook frames this as giving users a path forward: explain the limit specifically, offer an alternative, and hand back control with the context they need.

FailureWhat the user seesPatternMetric
Wrong answerFluent, confident, incorrectSources to check against; easy edit; one-click report with the context attachedEdit rate, reports per 1,000 answers
Incomplete resultPart of the task doneReport partial success explicitly: “7 of 10 updated; 3 failed, here’s why”Share of runs with silent partial failure
Wrong actionSomething changed that should not haveUndo, checkpoints, staged changes, delay before sendUndo rate, time to undo
RefusalThe system declinesNarrow refusal, say what it can do, offer the next stepOver-refusal rate on legitimate requests
Timeout or crashNothing, or a spinner foreverSaved state, resume, clear retryAbandonment after error

Design for undo

Undo is what makes higher autonomy safe (previous lessons). Build it into the action model:

  • Stage, then commit. Agents write to a draft, branch or pending state. The user or a rule promotes it.
  • Checkpoints. Record state before each agent step so a user can rewind to any point. Coding agents now commonly offer this for file edits.
  • Soft delete and delayed send. A 30-second send delay (illustrative) catches many mistakes at almost no cost.
  • Honest scope. If an action cannot be undone (an email delivered, a payment settled), say so at the approval step, and move that action down the autonomy dial.

Graceful refusal

Refusals fail in two directions. Under-refusal does harm. Over-refusal blocks legitimate work and teaches users the product is useless for a whole category. Both belong in your eval set (Chapter 5). When the system declines:

  • Decline the smallest part necessary and complete the rest.
  • Say what it can do, in one sentence, without lecturing.
  • Offer the next step: rephrase, a human, a different tool.
  • Avoid explaining exactly which rule fired when that would help someone get around it.

Recovery loops

The fastest recovery is usually an edit to the input. Keep the user’s prompt, attachments and settings after a failure. Offer “try again with…” options that change something meaningful (more context, a different source, a stricter format), because a plain regenerate often repeats the same mistake. For agents, let the user correct one step and resume from there.

Write the failures first

For any new AI flow, list the three most likely failures from error analysis on real or simulated outputs, and design each one to the same fidelity as the happy path. The deliverable for this chapter is that spec.

What changes for you

  • Add a failure section to every AI spec with the three most likely failures, what the user sees, the recovery path and the metric.
  • Make undo or staging a launch requirement for any action at “act” level. If it cannot be undone, it does not ship at that level.
  • Track over-refusal alongside harmful-output rates, and review refusal transcripts in your weekly error analysis.

lessons.t: Latency UX: streaming, progress and background work
lessons.html:
AI features are slow by the standards of normal software, and getting slower as reasoning and agent loops grow. Jakob Nielsen’s response-time limits still apply: about 0.1 seconds feels instant, about 1 second keeps the user’s train of thought, and about 10 seconds is the limit of attention on a single task. Beyond that, users need an estimate and something else to do. AI work now spans from under a second to hours, so one pattern cannot fit all of it.

DurationTypical AI workPattern
Under 1 sCompletion, classification, rankingNo indicator; use a small, fast model; precompute where possible
1–10 sA short answer, a single tool callStream tokens; show a subtle working state at once
10–60 sReasoning, multi-step retrievalShow stages as they happen (“searching 3 sources”, “checking totals”); let users keep working
MinutesAgent tasks, report generationRun in the background with a visible task list; notify on completion; allow cancel
HoursLong agent runs, batch jobsAsynchronous by design: inbox of tasks, partial results, resumable state, summary on return

Streaming

Streaming turns end-to-end latency into reading time, and time to first token (Chapter 1) becomes the number users feel. It has costs. You cannot validate a whole answer before showing it, so a guardrail that fires late forces you to retract text the user has read, which damages trust more than a short wait. Structured outputs such as tables or JSON stream awkwardly. Decide per surface: stream prose, buffer things that must be checked first.

Progress for thinking and acting

Reasoning models and agents can be silent for a long time. Show real progress: the plan, the step in progress, tools called, sources found. Avoid fake percentage bars, which users learn to distrust. Nielsen’s guidance holds: when total work is unknown, show progress in absolute terms, such as items processed. Speed of feedback also affects whether users trust the agent. In Anthropic’s February 2026 Claude Code study, the agent being slow, hanging or doing too much was the second most common reason humans interrupted it, at 17% of interruptions.

Background work

Once a task takes minutes, the design problem shifts from waiting to delegating. Background work needs:

  • A place where tasks live, with status, so users can leave and return.
  • Notifications that carry the result or the question itself.
  • Clean cancellation that leaves no half-finished state.
  • A way for the agent to ask a question without stalling silently, and for the user to answer from wherever they are.
  • A summary on return: what was done, what needs review, what failed.

Latency is a product dial

Model tier, reasoning budget and how many tool calls you allow all trade latency for quality and cost. Put the latency budget per surface in the spec (TTFT and end-to-end, at median and p95) and let the eval decide whether the slower option earns its time.

What changes for you

  • Specify latency per surface as TTFT and end-to-end at median and p95, plus which pattern from the table applies.
  • For anything over a minute, design the background experience (task list, notifications, cancel, summary) before the waiting experience.
  • Decide per surface whether to stream or buffer, based on whether output must be validated before a user sees it.

lessons.t: Steerability and feedback that actually improves the system
lessons.html:
Users need two kinds of control: steering this result now, and improving future results. Most products bolt on a thumbs button and call it both. It does neither well.

Steering, before, during and after

WhenMechanismExample
Before the runInstructions, settings, persistent preferences and project filesTone and length settings; a team style guide; AGENTS.md for coding agents
During the runInterrupt, redirect, answer the agent’s questions, queue a follow-upStop an agent heading the wrong way and give the missing fact
After the runEdit, refine with a constraint, regenerate one part“Shorter, and keep the second paragraph”

Mid-run steering matters more as runs get longer. In Anthropic’s Claude Code study, the most common reason humans interrupted was to provide missing technical context or corrections, about a third of interruptions. The agent also stopped itself to ask, most often to present a choice between approaches. Design both directions: the user can redirect easily, and the agent can ask a well-formed question and keep its state while it waits.

Feedback that carries information

SignalVolumeBiasBest use
Thumbs up or downLowSkews to extremes and to a few vocal usersFinding examples for error analysis
Edits to outputHighLow; users fix what they needMeasuring what was wrong, and building eval cases
Accept, reject, undoHighLow, but needs correctness labels to interpretAutonomy decisions and overreliance checks
Retry or rephraseMediumMixed; can be curiosityDetecting failed intents
AbandonmentHighAmbiguous on its ownSpotting broken flows, then reading transcripts

Microsoft’s Human-AI Interaction guidelines ask for granular feedback, learning from user behaviour, adapting cautiously, and telling users when the system changes. That last point is often missed. If feedback changes behaviour, say so (“we’ve stopped suggesting X”), or users conclude feedback is ignored and stop giving it.

Closing the loop

Feedback improves nothing until someone acts on it. A loop that works:

  1. Capture the signal with the full context: input, output, sources, model version, settings.
  2. Triage weekly in error analysis (Chapter 5): cluster failures by cause.
  3. Turn representative failures into eval cases.
  4. Fix at the cheapest rung of the behaviour-change ladder (Chapter 1).
  5. Confirm on the eval, ship, and tell users what changed.

This is the data flywheel from Chapter 7 at the UX layer. Check your privacy terms before using feedback content for training or evals.

Memory is steering too

If the product remembers preferences or facts about the user, show what it remembers, let users edit or delete it, and make clear when a memory shaped a result. Hidden memory that steers output feels like the system ignoring the user.

What changes for you

  • Instrument edits, accepts, rejects, undos and retries for every AI surface, with the context needed to replay the case.
  • Make “feedback to eval case” a weekly ritual with a named owner, and track how many cases each week came from users.
  • Ship a visible changelog or in-product note when user feedback changes behaviour.

lab.title: Redesign one flow at three points on the autonomy dial
lab.time: about half a day, plus five 30-minute user sessions
lab.intro: This lab tests whether more autonomy actually helps your users on one real flow, and how well each design holds up when the AI is wrong. You come out with evidence for the autonomy level to ship.
steps: Pick a flow. Choose one existing flow where AI could suggest, draft or act, with a clear task and a result you can check (for example, triaging a ticket, updating a record, drafting a reply). Write the user goal in one sentence.
Map the actions. List each action in the flow and score it for reversibility, blast radius and verification cost (low, medium, high).

Design three variants. Variant A suggests. Variant B drafts or acts with approval. Variant C acts and reports, with undo. Each variant includes its trust devices (sources, what was checked) and intervention controls.
Seed failures. Prepare five test tasks per variant. In two of the five, plant a realistic AI error: one obvious, one subtle. Keep the same tasks and errors across variants.
Prototype. Build clickable or working prototypes, with a coding agent if you like (Chapter 8). Responses can be scripted, but latency should match what production would deliver.
Run five users. Counterbalance the order of variants. Ask them to think aloud. Do not tell them errors are planted until the debrief.
Measure. For each variant: task time, errors caught, accept-when-wrong count, interventions used, and a 1–7 trust rating and preference at the end.
Decide. Pick the autonomy level per action class and write down the evidence. Note which failure each variant handled worst.
lab.template:
MeasureA: SuggestB: Draft or approveC: Act with undo
Median task time
Obvious errors caught (of 5)
Subtle errors caught (of 5)
Accept-when-wrong count
Undo or intervention used
Median trust rating (1–7)
Users preferring this variant
Worst-handled failure
lab.done: You have a filled table from five users, a chosen autonomy level for each action class with the reason, and a note on which failure the chosen design must handle better before launch. If the variant users preferred also had the highest accept-when-wrong count, you have found the trust problem to fix first.

quiz.q: Users approve 99% of an agent’s proposed calendar changes, taking about two seconds each. What should you do?
o: Nothing; high approval means the feature works
Add a second confirmation step for safety
Treat the approval as a rubber stamp: either automate with clear undo, or redesign the review view so people can actually check
Remove the feature, since users are not reading it
quiz.w: An approval that is always given in seconds is no longer a check. Calendar changes are reversible, so act with undo, or improve the review surface if they are risky.

quiz.q: A research assistant shows a confidence percentage on every answer. Error analysis shows the percentage barely tracks correctness. What is the better design?
o: Replace it with behaviours driven by system signals, such as asking, abstaining or flagging missing sources
Show the percentage in red when below 70%
Hide all uncertainty to avoid confusing users
Ask the model to be more careful in the system prompt
quiz.w: Model-stated confidence is poorly calibrated. Signals such as empty retrieval or sample disagreement, turned into visible behaviour, help users rely appropriately.

quiz.q: Which metric best tells you whether users are overrelying on an AI feature?
o: Overall acceptance rate
Thumbs-up rate
Time spent per session
Accept-when-wrong rate on labelled or seeded cases
quiz.w: Overall acceptance mixes useful acceptance with uncritical acceptance. Splitting by correctness isolates the errors users let through.

quiz.q: An agent updates 10 records, succeeds on 7 and fails on 3, then reports “Done”. What is the main design flaw?
o: The agent should have asked approval for each record
Silent partial failure; the result should state what succeeded, what failed and why, with a way to retry the failures
It should have rolled back all 10 records automatically
The progress bar was missing
quiz.w: Partial success is common in agent work. Reporting it explicitly and making the failed items easy to retry is the core recovery pattern.

quiz.q: Your compliance check runs on the full answer and occasionally blocks it. Answers currently stream. What is the risk, and the fix?
o: Streaming increases cost; turn it off everywhere
Users read text that is then retracted, which damages trust; buffer this surface or check in chunks before display
There is no risk if the check is fast
Show the blocked text with a warning
quiz.w: Streaming means you cannot validate before display. Where output must pass a check, buffer or validate incrementally, and accept the latency.

quiz.q: Users click thumbs-down often but quality is not improving. What is the most useful change?
o: Make the thumbs button larger
Add a five-star rating
Capture edits and rejections with full context, triage them weekly into eval cases, and tell users when behaviour changes
Fine-tune on every thumbs-down
quiz.w: Feedback improves nothing until it becomes eval cases and fixes. Edits carry more information than thumbs, and visible change keeps users giving feedback.

deliverable.title: Interaction spec: happy path and three likely failures
deliverable.html:
One page per AI flow, reviewed by design, engineering and the PM before build starts.

  1. User goal and flow. One sentence, then the happy path as numbered steps with what the user sees at each.
  2. Autonomy per action. A table of action classes with level (suggest, draft, act with approval, act), reversibility, blast radius, verification cost and measured reliability.
  3. Trust devices. Which sources are shown and how, the low-confidence behaviours, and what work the agent shows.
  4. Latency. TTFT and end-to-end budgets at median and p95, stream or buffer, and the background pattern if over a minute.
  5. Three likely failures. For each: how it was identified (error analysis, user test), what the user sees, the recovery path (edit, undo, retry, hand-off) and the metric with a threshold.
  6. Refusal behaviour. What the system declines, the copy pattern, and the next step offered.
  7. Steering and feedback. Controls before, during and after a run, the signals captured, and who turns them into eval cases each week.
  8. Launch checks. Accept-when-wrong rate, over-refusal rate, undo rate and abandonment after error, each with a target.

Attach the lab results as evidence for the autonomy levels chosen.
